talks.title: Practitioners' Perception of ML-Based Security Tools and Explanations
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Practitioners' Perception of ML-Based Security Tools and Explanations.
talks.summary:
Study Design

Jaron Mink (UIUC) presents interview findings on SOC practitioners’ views of ML-based security tools and explanations. Eighteen professionals with at least one year using classification tools participated in hour-long interviews covering backgrounds, ML usage, and three explanation types.

ML Plus Rules in Practice

Most SOCs combine ML with rule-based detection rather than using either alone. Rules anchor detection for known behaviors with lower false positives; ML supplements detection of novel activity but alone draws skepticism due to false-positive load.

Benefits and Pain Points

Practitioners weigh usability, effectiveness, adaptability, efficiency, and security. ML’s black-box outputs hinder trust, yet complex third-party rules are also opaque—“find who wrote the signal.” Hybrid approaches balance coverage and alert volume.

Explanations and Needs

Added ML explanations are evaluated against whether they resolve operational challenges. Correct classification under non-adversarial conditions remains the paramount unmet need; practitioners doubt ML alone meets SOC requirements despite industry AI hype.

talks.title: DVFS Frequently Leaks Secrets: Hertzbleed Attacks Beyond SIKE, Cryptography, and CPU-Only Data
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning DVFS Frequently Leaks Secrets: Hertzbleed Attacks Beyond SIKE, Cryptography, and CPU-Only Data.
talks.summary:
Hertzbleed Beyond SIKE

Researchers show DVFS-based Hertzbleed side channels extend past the broken SIKE protocol to patched cryptographic implementations and non-CPU components when power differences affect CPU frequency.

Amplification Requirement

Single-instruction Hamming-weight leaks are too small at millisecond DVFS granularity; attackers need gadgets that cumulatively change power draw, as in the original SIKE analysis.

Revived Crypto Targets

BearSSL ECDSA and classic McEliece implementations thought mitigated against prior side channels leak leading-zero nonce bits through timing when combined with existing lattice attacks.

GPU Cross-Component Leaks

Pixel-stealing SVG filter attacks thought fixed by constant-time GPU rendering can return because GPU power draw influences CPU frequency, letting JavaScript infer cross-origin iframe pixel colors.

talks.title: Bitcoin-Enhanced Proof-of-Stake Security: Possibilities and Impossibilities
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Bitcoin-Enhanced Proof-of-Stake Security: Possibilities and Impossibilities.
talks.summary:
Context

Anusratas presents joint work on Bitcoin-enhanced proof-of-stake security, motivated by Ethereum's merge and PoS goals: lower energy, faster confirmation, and validator accountability.

Accountability limits

Accountable safety identifies at least one-third double-signing validators after conflicting finalizations, but evolving stake and posterior-corruption attacks—publish attack chains only after unbonding—block slashable economic penalties for late-joining clients.

Babylon architecture

Pair a PoS chain with Bitcoin as a data-limited timestamping server; periodic succinct commitments (block hash + aggregated BLS signatures) anchor unbonding order so late clients can reject post-unbond attack chains.

Properties and costs

Babylon claims slashable safety, optimal resilience bounds, and improved liveness (one-third to one-half); experiments used hourly OP_RETURN timestamps (~$10K/year at $0.90 fees), but fee spikes could push costs toward ~$360K, driving aggregation across chains.

talks.title: Beyond Phish: Toward Detecting Fraudulent e-Commerce Websites at Scale
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Beyond Phish: Toward Detecting Fraudulent e-Commerce Websites at Scale.
talks.summary:
## Beyond Traditional Phishing Detection

Researchers at IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy present work on fraudulent e-commerce sites that steal payments without delivering goods. Unlike credential-phishing pages, these scams mimic legitimate storefronts—FTC-reported losses are substantial—and extend to fake pet-adoption and donation schemes.

## Building a Ground-Truth Dataset

The team collected roughly 29,000 online shopping sites, labeling about 23,100 legitimate and 6,100 fraudulent through manual verification. Category analysis of page source revealed scam typologies beyond simple brand impersonation, requiring features beyond URL similarity, logo presence, or login forms used in classic phishing detectors.

## Novel Detection Signals

Fraudulent sites often add social-media links to feign legitimacy, but behavioral patterns differ: inconsistent contact information, suspicious payment flows, and template reuse across unrelated "brands." Machine-learning models trained on these features outperform phishing-oriented classifiers on this domain.

## Scale and Responsible Disclosure

The system operates at web scale, surfacing persistent scams still online months later. Researchers reported findings to hosting providers and e-commerce platforms; Safe Browsing uptake varied. Code and data are released publicly to help hosting companies and security vendors protect consumers from payment fraud, not just credential theft.

talks.title: QueryX: Symbolic Query on Decompiled Code for Finding Bugs in COTS Binaries
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of QueryX: Symbolic Query on Decompiled Code for Finding Bugs in COTS Binaries.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Iyoung Sang Kang from Georgia Tech introduces QueryX, an extensible static checking tool that supports symbolic queries directly on decompiled code to discover vulnerabilities in commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) binaries. The research, conducted during Kang's PhD alongside colleagues Insu Yun and Taesoo Kim, tackles the scalability and accuracy trade-offs inherent in binary static analysis.

While extensible static analysis tools like CodeQL and Joern allow human analysts to write source-level queries, feeding decompiled code into them results in high false positive rates and missed bugs because source analyzers are unaware of underlying binary specifics (e.g., memory layout and data sections). Conversely, binary tools like angr and BAP rely on low-level binary intermediate representations (IR), which lack high-level abstractions like types and control flow, making queries complex and tedious to write. QueryX bridges this gap by enabling analysts to write high-level, analyst-friendly symbolic queries on decompiled code while remaining binary-aware.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Source and Binary Checkers**: Source-code query engines fed with decompiled code fail due to binary-unaware semantics like memory layouts and missing data sections. Binary IR tools (like angr) force analysts to deal with low-level details, resulting in verbose query code.
- **Decompiler Neutral Representation (DNR)**: QueryX introduces a new intermediate representation, DNR, to retain high-level decompiled code structures while injecting critical binary details, such as stack memory layouts and binary-embedded data sections.
- **Analyst-Friendly Symbolic Queries**: QueryX allows queries to be written using JavaScript syntax against decompiled code ASTs. Analysts can register execution callbacks on specific function calls (e.g., `malloc`, `memcpy`) to inspect symbolic states.
- **Real-World Bug Hunting in Windows Kernel**: Applying QueryX to the Windows kernel uncovered multiple zero-day vulnerabilities, including integer overflows that lead to heap buffer overflows.

### Technical Details
QueryX operates across four primary modules:
1. **Decompiler Module**: Takes target binaries and generates decompiled code (using Hex-Rays).
2. **Lifter Module**: Translates the decompiled code into DNR by calculating stack memory layouts, lifting stack variable accesses, and resolving global variable reads using a dedicated program data section that holds initial binary values and permissions.
3. **Query Interpreter**: Executes analyst queries written in JavaScript syntax, mapping query logic to decompiled AST nodes without forcing analysts to write queries against DNR directly.
4. **Analyzer Module**: Runs symbolic execution from function entry points, traversing AST nodes and firing registered callbacks (such as `collect_alloc` and `check_memcpy`). Callbacks read AST node values from the symbolic state and query the Z3 solver under current path constraints to detect issues like heap overflows.

In an evaluation comparing query complexity for a Windows kernel heap overflow caused by a 2-byte integer overflow, angr required 267 lines of code, whereas QueryX required only 33 lines due to its access to high-level decompiled type information. QueryX also outperformed Joern and CodeQL on a benchmark dataset by achieving higher true positives with fewer false positives.

### Takeaways
QueryX demonstrates that combining the high-level readability of decompiled code with binary-aware memory modeling yields practical, concise, and highly effective bug-finding queries. Applied to the Windows kernel across four query types, QueryX uncovered 15 new vulnerabilities (including 10 CVEs and 7 heap overflows), earning $180,000 in bug bounties. Future work noted during the Q&A includes further evaluating semantic equivalence between decompiled code and native binary code.

talks.title: User Perceptions and Experiences with Smart Home Updates
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding User Perceptions and Experiences with Smart Home Updates.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation details an empirical research study conducted in collaboration with Julie Haney at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) examining how consumers perceive and experience software and firmware updates for smart home IoT devices. With approximately half of U.S. households owning at least one IoT device, updates serve as a primary mechanism for manufacturers to patch security flaws and deliver functionality. However, consumer hesitation, disruption, and lack of technical savvy often impede timely patching. To address the lack of large-scale empirical studies in this area, the researchers surveyed 412 demographically diverse adult participants who were active users and administrators of smart home devices across five key categories: virtual voice assistants/smart speakers, smart thermostats, smart security devices, smart sensors, and smart lighting.

### Key Topics
- **Device Ownership and Category Differences**: Participants owned an average of nine smart devices, with 35% owning 10 or more. The study examined how perceptions varied across device types with varying levels of sophistication and perceived privacy/security exposure.
- **Perceptions of Update Importance and Urgency**: Assessing whether consumers view IoT device updates as critical and time-sensitive.
- **Current vs. Preferred Update Modes and Notifications**: How updates are handled (automatic vs. manual), how users are informed of new updates, and how they would prefer these mechanisms to work.
- **Security and Privacy Concerns**: Consumer trust in device security and privacy, and how concern levels correlate with update behaviors.

### Technical Details & Survey Findings
- **Importance and Urgency**: Overall, 86% of participants agreed that smart home updates are important, and 83% agreed they should be urgent. However, pairwise comparisons revealed significant differences: lighting updates were viewed as significantly less important and less urgent than other categories, while security devices were rated significantly more urgent and important than voice assistants.
- **Update Delivery Modes**: Automatic updates were the most commonly implemented method across all categories and were preferred for voice assistants and thermostats. In contrast, users preferred manual updates for security devices and sensors. Between 13% and 21% of respondents did not know how updates were currently handled on their devices.
- **User Agency and Preferences**: Over 50% of participants expressed a desire to choose between automatic and manual updates and to select their notification methods. Additionally, 40% wanted the capability to uninstall an update if it caused issues or disruptions. Companion apps were the most common and preferred notification channel, though roughly 25% reported having to learn about updates independently via social media, websites, or friends.
- **Security and Privacy Perceptions**: Only about one-third of participants were moderately or extremely concerned about security across all device categories. Voice assistants (perceived as always listening) and security devices elicited higher security and privacy concerns than thermostats, sensors, or lighting. Crucially, 77% of respondents believed their devices were secure, and 77% believed their devices actively protected their privacy—assumptions the speaker noted as surprisingly optimistic given typical IoT vulnerability profiles.

### Takeaways & Manufacturer Guidance
- **Transparency and Communication**: Manufacturers should clearly communicate the purpose of updates, when they are applied, and what changes they make, potentially leveraging cybersecurity labels to help non-technical consumers evaluate device security.
- **Configurable Control and Agency**: Rather than imposing a rigid, one-size-fits-all automatic update model, manufacturers should offer configurable options, such as choices between manual and automatic updates, scheduling installations for convenient times, and providing fallback/uninstall options when updates introduce compatibility or functionality defects.
- **Centralized Management**: To alleviate the burden of managing updates across dozens of devices, centralized apps or smart home hubs should consolidate notifications and coordinate update processes across multiple vendors.

talks.title: Private Eye: On the Limits of Textual Screen Peeking via Eyeglass Reflections in Video Conferencing
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Private Eye: On the Limits of Textual Screen Peeking via Eyeglass Reflections in Video Conferencing.
talks.summary:
### Overview
With the widespread adoption of video conferencing during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, eyeglass reflections pose an unintended side-channel vulnerability. The presentation introduces "Private Eye," a project that characterizes and quantifies the limits of information leakage from eyeglass reflections captured by participants' webcams. Termed a "webcam peeking attack," this threat involves a remote conference participant eavesdropping on the screen contents of another attendee without controlling the victim's hardware.

### Key Topics
- **Hardware & Computational Evolution:** Video cameras have transitioned from standard 720p laptop webcams and 1080p external cameras toward 4K streaming sensors. In parallel, adversaries can employ multi-frame super-resolution and image registration over consecutive frames to enhance reflection quality.
- **Environmental & Optical Factors:** Information leakage is influenced by reflection pixel size (governed by screen-to-glass distance, camera resolution, glass curvature) and signal-to-noise ratio (affected by ambient room lighting). Notably, auto-exposure controls cause lighting intensity to impact reflection clarity non-monotonically, and stronger prescription glasses with flatter surfaces leak more detail.
- **Text vs. Website Layout Recognition:** While reading small body text is difficult with existing hardware, identifying large texts or entire website layouts presents an immediate risk.

### Technical Details
- **Evaluation Methodology:** The study combined controlled laboratory experiments (single-letter tests) with user studies involving 20 participants viewing HTML text of varied sizes. Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were used as a baseline to humanly recognize reflected text, complemented by multi-frame super-resolution.
- **Text Leakage Limits:** With current webcams (720p/1080p), adversaries can read large fonts (roughly 56 pt or 10 mm physical height on screen, found on sites like Twitch). Predictive mathematical models indicate that future 4K webcams will allow peeking at most HTML header text, though body text remains challenging.
- **Website Identification:** Attackers can identify website layouts and shapes rather than specific text. On the Alexa Top 100 dataset, the researchers achieved over 90% accuracy in identifying the visited website (such as Bing) using present-day webcams.

### Mitigations & Takeaways
- **Individual Reflection Testing:** Platforms like Zoom could implement a per-session calibration test displaying known patterns to quantify current reflection risks and alert users.
- **Software Filtering:** The authors developed a Python prototype that detects the eyeglass area in the camera feed and applies an adjustable blur filter before streaming.
- **Principle of Least Pixels:** Treating this as an "over-sensing" issue where sensors capture more data than necessary, video conferencing systems should adopt a "principle of least pixels"—defaulting to lower resolutions and requiring deliberate user authorization for higher-capability video streams.

talks.title: PyFET: Forensically Equivalent Transformation for Python Binary Decompilation
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in PyFET: Forensically Equivalent Transformation for Python Binary Decompilation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
PyFET presents a novel technique for improving Python binary decompilation through Forensically Equivalent Transformations (FET). Developed via a joint collaboration between the University of Virginia, Georgia Tech, and the University of Tennessee Knoxville, PyFET addresses the problem of decompilation failures in Python malware binaries compiled to bytecode. Decompilers often fail or produce incorrect output when processing complex Python binaries. Instead of modifying or patching complex decompiler codebases, PyFET directly modifies and transforms the binary bytecode beforehand to make it compatible with existing decompilers.

### Key Topics
Decompilers encounter two primary categories of failures when processing Python binaries:
- **Explicit Errors:** Failures where the decompiler raises an error message, often providing hints such as approximate bytecode offsets or function names.
- **Implicit Errors:** Silent failures where decompilation finishes without warning but introduces semantic or structural corruptions. In a controlled study of 3,000 source files from PyPI and other repositories, researchers observed severe implicit bugs, including code coupled into incorrect scopes, unexpected `else` blocks injected into `try-except` statements, and while-loops inadvertently replaced with if-conditions.

To identify implicit errors, the authors developed a pattern-matching and mutation-based validation method. When a suspected pattern matches, the code is mutated with a corrected snippet, recompiled, and checked against the original binary at the target offset. This technique uncovered more than 22,000 previously undetected implicit errors across five decompilers.

### Technical Details
To fix binaries without triggering side effects in decompilers, PyFET introduces Forensically Equivalent Transformations (FETs), extending semantically equivalent transformations (SETs). When strict semantic equivalence fails to prevent decompiler crashes, FET relaxes semantics while preserving critical forensic context:
- **Transformation Rules:** PyFET utilizes 30 transformation rules targeting problem areas such as shortening lengthy conditional statements, dividing logical expressions, converting lambdas into standard functions, simplifying consecutive control flow, and moving statements (e.g., relocating a `return` statement outside a `with` block while capturing the result in a dedicated `fet_return` variable).
- **Iterative CFG Optimization:** Rather than transforming entire binaries indiscriminately, PyFET inspects the control flow graph (CFG). It starts at the failure node, applies applicable transformation rules, and progressively expands to adjacent nodes along connecting edges until decompilation succeeds or all paths are explored. This strategy limits auditing to approximately 33% of nodes.
- **Evaluation:** In an evaluation involving over 35,000 malware samples provided by ReversingLabs, 44.6% failed baseline decompilation, with failure rates rising on later Python versions. PyFET resolved more than 17,000 errors across five decompilers and successfully addressed binaries protected by obfuscators such as PyArmor/PJ Orion and opcode remapping.

### Takeaways
Attempting to build a single "perfect" Python decompiler or patch disparate decompiler engines creates significant maintenance overhead and regression risks. Transforming Python bytecode directly via forensically equivalent rules provides an effective, scalable pre-processing pipeline that dramatically boosts decompilation success across diverse decompilers and heavily obfuscated real-world malware.

talks.title: Membership inference attacks from first principles
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Membership inference attacks from first principles.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation explores membership inference attacks against machine learning models from first principles, aiming to determine whether a specific example was included in a target model's training set. The speaker explains that while directly computing the probability distribution of high-dimensional neural network weights is intractable, attackers can instead evaluate model loss on a specific input as a scalar value. By re-evaluating membership inference through per-example parametric distributions rather than single global thresholds, the authors present an attack that is both conceptually grounded and significantly more effective in high-precision regimes.

### Key Topics
- **Foundations of Membership Inference**: Framing membership inference as a statistical test comparing the probability that a model was trained on an example versus not trained on it.
- **Limitations of Weight-Space Modeling**: The computational impossibility of modeling distributions over million- or billion-dimensional neural network parameter spaces directly, motivating loss-based scalar metrics.
- **Per-Sample Distributions vs. Global Thresholds**: Demonstrating that different training examples (e.g., an image of a cat versus an airplane) have vastly different baseline loss distributions, making fixed, global decision thresholds inadequate.
- **Evaluation Flaws in Prior Work**: Critiquing the reliance on average-case accuracy across an entire dataset, which obscures whether an attack can reliably identify vulnerable individuals at low false positive rates (FPR).

### Technical Details
To estimate the loss distributions, the methodology trains multiple "shadow" models by masking subsets of the training data (typically 50% randomly masked per model). The models are partitioned into two sets for a target image: models that saw the example during training (IN) and models that did not (OUT). Computing the loss on the target image for each set yields two distinct empirical distributions.

While a non-parametric histogram would require training thousands of models (e.g., 10,000 models), the authors fit parametric Gaussian distributions to each set, reducing the requirement to approximately 16–32 models (or as few as 8). The crossing point of these fitted Gaussians provides a calibrated, per-example decision threshold. Furthermore, the likelihood ratio between the distributions provides a calibrated confidence estimate for any given prediction.

Evaluating across ROC curves in log-log scale reveals that prior attacks boasting high average accuracy (e.g., around 59%) perform essentially at random guessing at low false positive rates (<10% FPR). In contrast, the proposed method outperforms prior work both on average accuracy and dramatically at low FPR regimes. The paper also supports both an "online" variant (training models specifically with/without the query point) and an "offline" variant that performs almost as well without retraining per query point.

### Takeaways
The speaker highlights a critical conclusion: many existing beliefs in the membership inference literature may need to be re-evaluated. Prior claims that certain defenses (such as weight decay) are ineffective were established only against weak, average-case global threshold attacks, leaving open whether they protect against strong attacks operating at low false positive rates. The primary trade-off of the proposed approach is the computational cost of training multiple models, though its principles also extend downstream to attribute inference and data extraction.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Arvind, a postdoctoral researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, presents joint research with Giulio (MPI) and Pedro (IMDEA) on universal atomic swaps across blockchains. Cross-currency token exchange is a fundamental economic activity, yet existing trustless solutions struggle with atomicity—ensuring that either both parties receive their swapped coins or neither does. Traditional solutions rely on centralized exchange services (which require high availability and risk coin theft), third-party smart contract blockchains (which can be complex and expensive), or Hashed Time-Locked Contracts (HTLCs) within payment channels. However, HTLCs rely on specialized scripting, limiting interoperability with simpler blockchains, incurring high on-chain fees, and degrading token fungibility. The authors introduce a universal, multi-asset atomic swap protocol that eliminates the need for HTLCs and special scripts, requiring only standard signature verification scripts.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of HTLCs**: HTLCs require specialized script support, increase on-chain transaction costs, and harm token fungibility because transactions stand out on-chain.
- **Multi-Asset Atomicity Notion**: In multi-asset exchanges, traditional definitions can allow a malicious party to claim a subset of coins and refund their own assets. The proposed model enforces that if Alice claims even a single coin on her side, Bob is guaranteed the ability to claim all coins on his side.
- **Adaptor Signatures**: A cryptographic primitive defined over an NP relation and signature scheme that links signature validity to the revelation of a witness, allowing off-chain atomic linkage.
- **Verifiable Timed Discrete Logarithms (VTD Log)**: A cryptographic commitment tool used to replace on-chain lock-time/timeout scripts for handling refunds privately and off-chain.

### Technical Details
The core construction focuses on Schnorr and ECDSA signatures and operates across four main phases:
1. **Setup Phase**: Alice and Bob establish payment channels where channel addresses are shared public keys with distributed secret key shares. To handle timeouts without on-chain lock-time scripts, parties exchange Verifiable Timed Discrete Logarithm (VTD log) commitments to their secret key shares (set to duration $T$ for Alice and $T + \Delta$ for Bob), which both parties begin brute-forcing immediately.
2. **Lock Phase**: Alice selects a statement-witness pair for an NP relation. Using a two-party computation protocol, Bob obtains pre-signatures for his outgoing transactions under Alice's statement. Similarly, pre-signatures are generated for Alice's incoming transactions using the identical statement instance.
3. **Swap Complete Phase**: Alice uses her witness to adapt the pre-signatures into valid signatures, publishing them on-chain to claim her coins. Bob observes the published signature on any blockchain, extracts the underlying witness using the adaptor signature extraction algorithm, adapts his own pre-signatures, and posts them to claim all corresponding coins on his side.
4. **Timeout Phase**: If the swap does not complete, users finish brute-forcing the VTD log commitments after time $T$ (or $T + \Delta$). Recovering the counterparty's key share gives the party the full channel private key, enabling immediate unilateral refund of unswapped coins via standard transactions without revealing lock-time scripts or channel expiry logic on-chain.

### Takeaways
The proposed universal atomic swap construction makes cross-chain swap transactions look like ordinary payment transactions, lowering on-chain gas costs (demonstrated on Ethereum) and protecting token fungibility and privacy across any cryptocurrency supporting basic digital signatures. Open problems include mitigating denial-of-service risks where participants go offline to trigger refunds, and achieving scriptless atomic swaps that allow unconditional redemption regardless of timeouts.

talks.summary:
## Overview
Nostar is a verified implementation framework for the Noise protocol family, a collection of approximately 59 protocols (expandable with new features) used for key exchange and contract establishment. Noise protocols are already deployed in real-world applications like WhatsApp and WireGuard VPN. The core problem Nostar addresses is that while many Noise implementations exist across programming languages, none are formally verified, leaving them vulnerable to bugs commonly discovered in protocol implementations (such as TLS and Signal).

## Technical Architecture
Nostar comprises three integrated components:

1. **Protocol Compiler**: Transforms Noise protocol patterns into specialized, verified C implementations
2. **Verified Library Stack**: Provides a high-level defensive API exposing memory-safe, type-safe, and functionally correct code
3. **Formal Security Analysis**: Uses symbolic methods to prove authentication and confidentiality guarantees

The verification toolchain builds on F* (a theorem prover with dependent types and program verification) and Low* (an effectful subset for writing verified C-like code), with compilation to C via the Karamel framework. This approach has been successfully applied in the Everest project for providing verified HTTPS components.

## Key Innovation: Partial Evaluation
The central technical contribution is using partial evaluation to transform a generic interpreter-based specification into specialized compiled code. Rather than writing separate implementations for each protocol, the speaker describes a technique where:
- A single High* interpreter processes protocol token lists
- Low* rewrites this interpreter with preconditions, postconditions, and functional correctness properties linked to the high-level spec
- At compile-time, F* specializes the code by inlining the interpreter, evaluating matches, and eliminating recursive calls

F*'s dependent type system enables extremely precise control flow with no runtime token processing or list manipulation. The speaker compares this to C++ template metaprogramming applied at the protocol definition level, using partial reduction techniques previously employed in cryptographic primitives like Hacl* and vectorization code.

## API Design and Security Properties
The high-level API (accounting for over 75% of generated code) implements:
- Verified state machines abstracting handshake and transport phases
- Misuse-resistant patterns that prevent sending data before security guarantees are established
- Dynamic checks and verified key management utilities for validation, loading, and secure storage

Security analysis is formalized in Dollar* (a photosymbolic analysis framework), with one generic symbolic proof operating at the interpreter specification level. This enables analysis of all 59 protocols simultaneously, in contrast to tools like ProVerif that typically require per-protocol proofs.

## Implementation Results
The framework generated code for all 59 Noise patterns with 8 cipher suite variants each, totaling 472 instantiations. Benchmarks show competitive performance against existing implementations, with execution speed superior to all tested alternatives except WireGuard (which is hand-optimized for a single pattern).

## Limitations and Q&A Clarifications
Formal proofs cover functional correctness and some constant-time properties (by avoiding operations like division), but do not extend to C compiler behavior or memory-zeroing guarantees (which are implemented manually). Adding new protocols at the pattern layer is straightforward, but extending the API or updating security proofs requires more substantial work due to subtle symbolic analysis constraints.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Patrick presents Blacksmith, a scalable Rowhammer testing tool and fuzzer operating in the frequency domain. As DRAM scaling has significantly reduced the activation threshold required to trigger bit flips—dropping from roughly 139,000 activations in DDR3 (2012) to around 10,000 activations in newer DDR4 devices (mid-2019)—DRAM manufacturers like Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron deployed in-DRAM mitigations called Target Row Refresh (TRR). TRR mechanisms attempt to estimate frequently hammered rows and inject preventive refreshes before data loss occurs. However, Blacksmith demonstrates that existing TRR mitigations across major DDR4 and LPDDR4X devices are fundamentally flawed.

### Key Topics
- **Target Row Refresh (TRR) Limitations**: TRR mitigations rely on frequent item count algorithms implemented under strict silicon area and timing constraints, often without formal security analysis. They typically comprise a sampler (which tracks activation frequencies) and an inhibitor (which issues preventive refreshes).
- **Limitations of Uniform Hammering**: Prior attacks primarily used uniform n-sided patterns where all aggressors were accessed at identical frequencies, allowing sampler heuristics to track them easily.
- **Frequency-Domain Rowhammering**: By systematically exploring non-uniform access patterns, the authors mapped critical attack parameters into frequency-domain properties: phase (timing/offset relative to refresh commands), amplitude (hammering intensity or peak access count), and frequency (hammering across multiple refresh intervals).
- **Blacksmith Fuzzer**: A generic, extensible fuzzing framework that crafts complex patterns combining varied frequencies, phases, and amplitudes to systematically trigger bit flips.

### Technical Details
- **Timing Window Constraints**: DRAM relies on JEDEC standard DDR timing, requiring cell retention for at least 64 ms with periodic refresh commands sent approximately every 7.8 µs on DDR4. In an interval between consecutive refreshes, an attacker can issue roughly 166 activations, summing to around 1.3 million activations across a full 64 ms refresh window.
- **Parametric Observations**:
  - *Phase/Timing*: Testing on Samsung DIMM A10 showed bit flips only occurred when aggressor pairs were hammered immediately before a refresh command, suggesting sampler inactivity prior to refresh.
  - *Amplitude/Intensity*: Increasing hammering intensity boosted bit flips only up to a sweet spot; exceeding it caused flips to drop because the sampler detected the aggressor and triggered TRR.
  - *Frequency/Pattern Length*: Extending patterns over multiple refresh intervals (e.g., hammering heavily only every second interval) was necessary to induce flips on specific hardware, such as SK Hynix DIMM B2.
- **Evaluation Results**: Evaluated against 40 test devices from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, Blacksmith triggered bit flips on 100% (40/40) of the devices, outperforming Trespass (which triggered flips on 15/40). On a Samsung device (A17), Blacksmith produced roughly 138,000 bit flips. Additionally, all tested LPDDR4X devices were vulnerable.
- **Exploitation**: Using established attack patterns, page table entry (PTE) exploits succeeded on 30 of 40 devices, yielding exploitable bit flips within three seconds to two hours and eight minutes.
- **Generalization**: When approached by an unstudied vendor with an unanalyzed proprietary DDR4 device, Blacksmith discovered bit flips in less than four hours.

### Takeaways
Current proprietary, obscure TRR implementations deployed by DRAM manufacturers fail to prevent Rowhammer bit flips under non-uniform, frequency-domain access patterns. The speaker concludes that hardware vendors must transition away from ad-hoc mitigations toward principled defenses with provable security guarantees, citing research such as ProTRR.

### Overview
In this talk, Sanjay presents a systematization of knowledge regarding software-based defenses against Spectre attacks. Spectre fundamentally breaks standard processor execution assumptions by exploiting speculative execution mechanisms—such as branch predictors, return target predictors, indirect jump predictors, and memory disambiguation/data flow prediction. Because early mitigation efforts relied on ad hoc, reactive patches that failed to cover slightly altered attack patterns or cross-process mistraining, the speaker advocates for formal methods, principled attacker models, and domain-appropriate abstractions to systematically eliminate speculative leaks.

### Key Topics
- **Mechanisms of Spectre**: Out-of-order execution, branch misprediction bypassing memory bounds checks, indirect jump prediction, function return prediction, and data-flow store-to-load forwarding.
- **Limitations of Early Defenses**: Flaws in ad hoc solutions such as pattern matching in compilers (e.g., Microsoft's QSpecter flag), recurring manual kernel patches (Linux eBPF), and browser mitigations (Google Chrome's strict site isolation undermined by Spook.js).
- **Attacker Modeling and Abstraction Sweet Spots**: Why models that are too narrow (e.g., step-counter leakage models or influence-only models like 007) miss critical attacks like port contention or cross-process training, whereas overly expressive models (Constantine, Foundations, Inspector) introduce excessive false positives.
- **Domain-Specific Approaches**: Translating sequential security definitions into speculative semantics for cryptographic code (constant-time models) and sandboxed environments (e.g., WebAssembly, Linux eBPF).
- **Multi-Layer Verification and Compilation**: Establishing secure translation from high-level languages (C, Rust, Haskell) down through intermediate representations to structured assembly and machine code.

### Technical Details
The speaker highlights two primary application domains where formal software defenses have shown success:
1. **Cryptographic Software**: Building on sequential constant-time security (where execution traces and memory access patterns do not depend on secret data), tools like those in High-Assurance Cryptography and Hunting the Haunter extend constant-time semantics to speculative execution paths. Because cryptographic code tends to feature regular control flow and structured data, tracking speculative misprediction paths is mathematically tractable.
2. **Sandboxed Systems**: In environments like Linux eBPF and browser WebAssembly/JavaScript, sandboxes treat any out-of-bounds read as an immediate leak. Tools like FaCT/FEniCS-style systems, FaSym, or Swivel leverage sandbox host control to rewrite code and eliminate dangerous speculative paths.

More generalized tools such as Spectector and FaST adopt relative non-interference: programs running speculatively must not leak any more information than they would under normal sequential execution. To restore broader properties destroyed by Spectre (memory safety, type safety, and control flow integrity), research spans several abstraction layers:
- **Binary/Assembly Level**: Verified by tools such as Binsec and Spectector.
- **Structured Assembly & IR**: Tools like Jasmin, Blade, and FaCT work at structured assembly or LLVM IR, inserting barriers or transformations.
- **Sandboxed IR / High-Level Languages**: Swivel validates WebAssembly transformations. Blade establishes formal semantics between LLVM IR and assembly to prove that the resulting machine code remains Spectre-free, while hardware-software contracts bridge the gap between software semantics and hardware guarantees.

### Takeaways
To achieve sound, long-term software defenses against speculative execution vulnerabilities, security must be rebuilt from the ground up using formal methods rather than reactive patching. Developers and security architects must select attacker models tailored to their domain (e.g., constant-time for crypto, strict isolation for sandboxing) to avoid false positives and missed attacks. The ultimate goal is end-to-end, compiler-verified preservation of sequential security properties from high-level source languages down to hardware.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this WOOT 2021 keynote presentation, Dr. Sara Rampazzi, an assistant professor at the University of Florida and member of the Florida Institute for Cybersecurity, examines sensor security within the growing ecosystem of the Internet of Everything (IoE). As autonomous cyber-physical systems and artificial intelligence increasingly make critical decisions without direct human supervision, they fundamentally rely on sensors to perceive their surroundings. However, physical sensors and electronic components possess vulnerabilities stemming from physical phenomena that allow external analog signals—such as light, sound, and electromagnetic interference—to alter device behavior and manipulate higher-level software and machine learning models without requiring conventional software compromise or malware.

### Key Topics
- **The Internet of Everything and Autonomous Decisions**: How connected devices, smart homes, healthcare devices, and autonomous vehicles rely on sensors to gather environmental data for automated actions.
- **Sensor Exploitation Mechanisms**: Five core physical factors exploited by attackers: coupling (e.g., resonant frequency EMI), non-linearities in hardware components, intermodulation/frequency generation, predictable periodic behavior/timing, and over-sensing/accidental transduction.
- **Signal Injection via Light (MEMS Microphones)**: Demonstrating how voice-controllable systems (Google Home, Amazon Echo, Facebook Portal, smartphones, tablets) can be commanded using amplitude-modulated lasers.
- **Downstream System Compromise**: Leveraging compromised voice assistants to execute actions across connected IoT ecosystems, such as unlocking smart locks, opening garage doors, and starting cars.
- **Autonomous Vehicle Perception Spoofing**: Attacking LiDAR systems using precise timing and relay attacks to feed fake echo signals into obstacle-detection systems, fooling machine learning perception frameworks (like Baidu Apollo).
- **Hardware-Software Co-Design for Defense**: Moving past isolated software patches and appreciating the physical reality of hardware to engineer resilient defenses.

### Technical Details
- **MEMS Microphone Light Vulnerability**: MEMS microphones contain a movable diaphragm and a stationary back plate forming a parallel-plate capacitor, coupled to an onboard ASIC. Due to photoacoustic and photoelectric effects across the membrane and ASIC, incoming light irradiance induces measurable voltage changes. Modulating the current driving a laser diode with an amplified audio signal creates an amplitude-modulated light beam that translates into clear voltage signals mimicking acoustic voice commands.
- **Attack Range and Penetration**: Using optics and a low-power 5 milliwatt laser pointer setup (achievable with setups as cheap as ~$300), commands were successfully delivered through windows and between buildings up to 110 meters away across more than 17 tested devices.
- **Compounding IoT Flaws**: Light injection attacks succeeded in manipulating downstream infrastructure due to weak default configurations, lack of authentication on multi-user speakers, bypassable voice personalization (via text-to-speech spoofing), routine automations bypassing PIN entry, and lack of brute-force rate limiting on spoken PINs.
- **LiDAR Spoofing and Adversarial Injection**: LiDAR determines distance by timing reflected laser pulses. By exploiting sensor periodicity, synchronized relay attacks injected false reflections, projecting an adversarial horizontal line that tricked the Apollo autonomous driving perception model into detecting nonexistent obstacles, stopping simulated and moving vehicles.

### Takeaways
- Sensors serve as both the primary target and an entry medium to compromise all layers of a system, from silicon to machine learning models.
- Traditional security countermeasures (cryptography, memory safety, software patching) cannot remediate physical over-sensing vulnerabilities once hardware is deployed.
- Mitigations require a layered defense combining hardware modifications (e.g., non-exposed acoustic ports, shielded boards), multi-sensor input validation, and anomaly detection algorithms.
- Security researchers, hardware manufacturers, and software engineers must break down domain silos and treat hardware and software as a single unified system to anticipate emerging attacks.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, James Roney presents research on enhancing memory cartography—a specialized data-oriented attack technique—to identify valuable pointers in heap memory without requiring heap spraying. In a standard memory cartography attack, an attacker with an arbitrary memory read vulnerability navigates through an application's address space along a pre-mapped network of pointers between memory regions (such as static data sections, heaps, and stacks) to leak arbitrary sensitive data without causing segmentation faults. While static data sections maintain deterministic relative layouts despite Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), transitioning from a dynamic, non-deterministic heap allocation to static data sections originally relied on heap spraying predictable objects. Roney and his collaborators introduce a method that uses signature-based byte filtering to reliably identify pointers from uncontrolled heap regions to static data sections.

### Key Topics
- **Data-Oriented Attacks vs. Control-Flow Hijacking**: Unlike traditional control-flow hijacking attacks (e.g., overwriting return addresses) that trigger modern defenses such as stack canaries or Control Flow Integrity (CFI), data-oriented attacks manipulate program variables and data pointers while strictly adhering to legitimate control-flow paths.
- **Memory Cartography Mechanics**: Originally introduced by Rogowski et al., memory cartography creates an offline map of deterministic pointers between memory regions. By chaining these references, an attacker can traverse from an initial leak to target data (such as browser session cookies) across fragmented memory spaces.
- **Heap Non-Determinism Limitation**: Previous memory cartography required spraying known objects into the heap to bridge the gap between dynamic heap memory and static sections. In environments where the attacker cannot control heap allocations, this method fails.
- **Signature-Based Pointer Identification**: An offline analysis technique that characterizes the byte patterns immediately surrounding frequent pointers to static destinations, generating simple byte-level filters that can identify target pointers during runtime heap scanning.

### Technical Details
- **Offline Signature Compilation**: The attacker executes the target application locally multiple times across independent runs with ASLR enabled. By inspecting boundaries (e.g., via Linux `/proc/self/maps`), the attacker tracks heap memory regions and maps all pointers referencing external targets (such as libc or program libraries). The method identifies the most frequently referenced destination offsets across runs. For each target destination, the algorithm inspects a window of bytes surrounding the pointers (preceding bytes, pointer bytes shifting due to ASLR, and trailing bytes) and establishes upper and lower bound value intervals for each position across all runs to construct a byte filter.
- **Online Attack Execution**: At attack time, the attacker scans memory starting from their local heap read vulnerability and evaluates aligned pointer-sized regions against the pre-compiled byte bounds. Once a match is detected, the attacker extracts the pointer to the known static destination, anchoring their memory cartography navigation without crashing the process.
- **Empirical Evaluation**: The approach was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation across 10 memory dumps per target program:
  - *Vim*: Tested as a single-threaded baseline with a unified heap; identified pointers to top frequent destinations with over 99% precision.
  - *Firefox*: Characterized by complex, multi-VMA jemalloc heap chunks. By aggregating relevant jemalloc chunks matching the JavaScript heap, the filter identified pointers to `libxul` with high precision, maintaining strong performance even in the worst-case individual heap chunk.
  - *Apache with OpenSSL 1.0.1 (Heartbleed)*: Evaluated against a real-world read vulnerability scenario, demonstrating equally high precision.

### Takeaways
- **Expanded Threat Surface**: Attackers can reliably locate entry points into static data structures from heap memory using passive signature matching, eliminating the prerequisite of heap spraying.
- **Security Implications**: Highlights the critical need for strict process isolation and independent address spaces for mutually untrusted origins, as in-process mitigations and ASLR do not prevent data-oriented pointer mapping.
- **Assumptions & Future Directions**: The technique relies on stability of inter-region offsets between local analysis environments and victim targets. Future work aims to evaluate complete end-to-end exploits under real-world timing and bandwidth constraints.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines the viability of achieving privacy-preserving machine learning through instance encoding, focusing on the InstaHide scheme introduced at ICML. Instance encoding adds a pre-processing step where training data is converted into intermediate encodings intended to prevent information leakage while enabling models to train directly on the encoded data. The authors evaluate InstaHide's empirical security by completely breaking its official challenge dataset, present theoretical impossibility results bounding instance encoding privacy when combined with accuracy, and critically assess the role of security challenges in machine learning security research.

### Key Topics
- **Instance Encoding in Machine Learning:** The concept of transforming raw training data into privacy-preserving intermediate encodings that allow downstream algorithms to train without direct access to private samples.
- **InstaHide Architecture:** A mechanism combining linear combinations of private images with samples from an unlabeled public dataset, followed by random pixel sign flipping (masking).
- **Attack on the InstaHide Challenge:** A practical reconstruction attack utilizing neural-network-based clustering followed by image recovery to reconstruct private training images.
- **Theoretical Barriers:** Formal security definitions and impossibility theorems demonstrating fundamental trade-offs between instance encoding accuracy and cryptographic privacy.
- **Evaluation of Security Challenges:** The limitations of relying on static empirical challenges without formal, falsifiable security models and threat definitions.

### Technical Details
- **InstaHide Encoding Mechanism:** InstaHide draws images from both a private labeled dataset and an auxiliary public dataset, creates a linear combination of these images, and applies a masking layer that randomly flips the sign of each pixel with probability 1/2.
- **Challenge Reconstruction Attack:** The InstaHide challenge provided 50 encodings for each of 100 private images using an undisclosed public dataset. The attack operates in two phases: first, a neural network clusters encodings based on the underlying private images they encode; second, an image recovery step reconstructs the original images from each cluster, achieving near-perfect recovery of all 100 challenge images.
- **Alternative Threat Model Attack:** Assuming auxiliary knowledge where the attacker has access to the public dataset used during encoding, the authors developed an efficient attack that scales linearly with data size and reconstructs a private image from just a single encoding.
- **Theoretical Impossibility Bounds:** The authors formulated a security game where an adversary distinguishes which of two identically labeled instances was encoded. They proved that if a protocol achieves accuracy 1/2 + ε on encoded data across two concept functions, a polynomial-time adversary achieves advantage 1/2 + Ω(ε) in breaking privacy. When accuracy is defined on original data, the adversary's advantage is bounded by 1/2 + 1/n (where n is sample complexity), ruling out cryptographic levels of privacy.

### Takeaways
- **InstaHide is Insecure:** InstaHide fails to provide robust privacy, as demonstrated by the complete reconstruction of its official challenge dataset and efficient single-encoding recovery under public dataset knowledge.
- **Fundamental Incompatibility:** Strong cryptographic privacy and high utility/accuracy cannot be achieved simultaneously via instance encoding alone.
- **Challenges Cannot Replace Formal Models:** Security challenges should serve only as necessary conditions for security and cannot substitute for clear threat models and falsifiable claims. The broader machine learning security field must transition from informal evaluations toward rigorous, mathematically defined threat models.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Itay Tsabary presents "MAD-HTLC: Because HTLC is Crazy-Cheap to Attack," joint work with Matan Yechieli, Alex Manuskin, and Ittay Eyal. Hash Time Lock Contracts (HTLCs) are standard smart contract primitives fundamental to off-chain scaling solutions like the Lightning Network, atomic swaps, and contingent payments. While previously known to be vulnerable to miner bribery attacks on Ethereum via complex smart contracts, this research demonstrates that bribery attacks against HTLCs are simpler, cheaper, and directly applicable to Bitcoin via standard transaction fees. To resolve this vulnerability systematically, the authors propose MAD-HTLC, an incentive-compatible replacement based on the game-theoretic principle of Mutually Assured Destruction.

### Key Topics
- **HTLC Miner Bribery Vulnerability:** HTLC security relies on the assumption that a valid preimage transaction published before timeout $T$ will be confirmed. However, this ignores miner extractable value (MEV). A sender (Batman) can bribe miners with higher transaction fees to delay the recipient's (Antman's) transaction until the timeout elapses, stealing the locked funds.
- **Subgame Perfect Equilibrium (SPE) Analysis:** Using backward induction to model the game across rounds, the authors prove that when all miners are rational, attack bribery costs are independent of the timeout duration $T$, invalidating the assumption that longer timeouts mitigate attacks.
- **MAD-HTLC Architecture:** A protocol leveraging miner incentives as deterrence. If both parties' preimages are exposed, any miner can claim the entire locked balance as MEV, ensuring both parties lose if an attack is attempted.
- **Bitcoin MEV Feasibility:** Demonstrating through Bitcoin Core patches that implementing MEV and bribery logic requires minimal code and is practical today.

### Technical Details
- **Cost & Empirical Findings:** Analysis revealed Bitcoin HTLCs securing over $26,000 where an attacker could pull off the bribery attack for a cost of merely $2. If the honest party attempts a counter-bribe bidding war, they require a linear fee of roughly 1% of the locked value (e.g., $260 on a $26,000 balance, which is 10,000 times higher than typical transaction fees).
- **MAD-HTLC Design:** Built using two subcontracts (split for Bitcoin Script, consolidatable in Ethereum Solidity):
  1. *Deposit Contract:* Redeemed by Antman presenting preimage 1, by Batman after timeout $T$ presenting preimage 2, or by *any miner* presenting both preimage 1 and preimage 2.
  2. *Collateral Contract (Optional):* Prevents a spiteful Batman from releasing preimage 2 after Antman claims the deposit; Batman reclaims it after timeout $T$, unless both preimages are revealed, in which case miners take the collateral.
- **Security & Incentive Proofs:** Formally modeled using an ideal functionality $\mathcal{F}$ and real hybrid protocol $\Pi$ using universal composability principles, proving indistinguishability alongside SPE game analysis.
- **Overhead & Mainnet Evaluation:** The Bitcoin Script implementation adds an overhead of only a few dollars. Ethereum Solidity has an overhead of roughly $150, reducible to ~$10 when amortized. Deployments on mainnets showed Ethereum transactions were front-run (MEV active), while Bitcoin transactions confirmed smoothly without MEV interference.
- **Bitcoin Core Patches:** To show MEV feasibility on Bitcoin, authors patched Bitcoin Core with a 150-LOC patch to coordinate bribe recognition and transaction delaying, and a 350-LOC patch establishing an external Python RPC infrastructure for custom MEV logic.

### Takeaways
Increasing HTLC timeouts does not protect against rational miner bribery, and relying on the current immaturity of Bitcoin MEV is dangerous. MAD-HTLC provides a practical, drop-in replacement that aligns miner incentives to guarantee protocol execution with negligible fee overhead.

### Overview
In this talk, security researcher Jorge Toro presents collaborative research conducted with David Basin and Ralph Sasse at ETH Zurich analyzing the EMV standard (commonly known as chip and PIN). With over 9 billion EMV smart cards in circulation worldwide, the standard is intended to safeguard high-value purchases through PIN verification known only to the legitimate cardholder. Using formal methods, the researchers developed the first comprehensive model of EMV to discover existing and new security issues, notably identifying and practically demonstrating a critical PIN bypass vulnerability in contactless Visa transactions, followed by proposing machine-checked fixes.

### Key Topics
- **EMV Protocol Architecture:** The breakdown of EMV transactions into four core phases: initial application selection and data exchange, offline data authentication (via SDA, DDA, or CDA), cardholder verification methods (offline PIN, online PIN, or Consumer Device Cardholder Verification Method / CDCVM), and transaction authorization (offline terminal acceptance or online issuer authorization).
- **Formal Verification with Tamarin:** Modeling protocol execution paths using multiset rewriting rules and verifying security properties expressed in first-order logic formulas, such as 'bank accepts', 'authentication to the terminal', and 'authentication to the bank' (formalized via injective agreement).
- **Contact EMV Findings:** Confirmation that only transactions combining Combined Dynamic Data Authentication (CDA) with online PIN or no PIN are secure, whereas transactions relying on offline PIN remain susceptible to PIN bypass attacks previously reported in 2010.
- **Contactless EMV & Visa PIN Bypass:** Uncovering that common MasterCard contactless transactions are secure, while common Visa transactions omit cryptographic signatures on Card Transaction Qualifiers (CTQ), allowing an attacker to tamper with the cardholder verification method.

### Technical Details
In the Visa contactless protocol, the card specifies its preferred Cardholder Verification Method (CVM) inside a data object known as Card Transaction Qualifiers (CTQ). Although the specification supports signing the CTQ using Signed Dynamic Authentication Data (SDAD), standard Visa transactions do not mandate or verify this signature. As a result, the CTQ lacks integrity protection.

The researchers weaponized this flaw by constructing an Android application operating a man-in-the-middle attack over a relay architecture. During a high-value purchase where the terminal requests cardholder verification, a genuine card responds indicating that an online PIN is required. The attacker intercepts and modifies the CTQ to indicate that cardholder verification was performed on a consumer device (CDCVM, typical for smartphones or smartwatches). The payment terminal accepts the transaction under the assumption that the user authenticated on a mobile device, completing the purchase without PIN entry. The authors demonstrated this live using a 200 Swiss franc transaction.

To remediate the vulnerability, the authors proposed activating the card's SDAD signature by flipping a single bit in one of the terminal's commands. Because this change is implemented on the terminal side, it does not require replacing existing cards in circulation. Other findings, such as attacks against offline low-value transactions that lead terminals to accept charges later rejected by issuing banks, lack authentication and require card reissuance to resolve.

### Takeaways
The findings highlight that human analysis alone cannot manage the branching complexity and state space of critical real-world protocols. Formal protocol verification using tools such as Tamarin should be integrated directly into development and standardization processes to identify and resolve vulnerabilities before mass deployment.

### Overview
In this presentation, Nicolas Swearman discusses research on interaction problems between password managers and websites. While password managers are recommended to alleviate the burden of memorizing unique, randomly generated credentials, their real-world operation relies heavily on browser extensions that inspect web pages and inject authentication functionality. Due to the complexity of website architectures and varying implementations of login and registration forms, password managers frequently fail to detect fields or properly autofill credentials.

### Key Topics
- **Password Reuse and User Perceptions**: According to a February 2019 online survey, 69% of participants believed they were very good at protecting online accounts and 59% believed they were safer than average. However, 52% admitted to reusing passwords across multiple accounts, 13% reused passwords for all accounts, and only 24% reported using a password manager.
- **Dataset and Issue Mining**: The researchers collected user-reported bugs across open-source repositories and extension stores, gathering 1,300 reviews across 15 password managers on the Chrome Web Store, 400 GitHub issues, and 729 Chrome Web Store support requests. Three authors filtered these reports for website interaction issues, establishing a codebook that yielded 152 relevant issues.
- **Categorization and Minimal Working Examples**: From the 152 issues, the authors identified 7 broad categories and 39 distinct problematic interaction patterns. They constructed minimal working examples (MWEs)—simplified HTML snippets isolating the specific form or script interaction (e.g., Google's two-page login flow)—to systematically evaluate password manager behavior.
- **Automated Testing Setup**: Testing was performed using an automated Selenium script that launched clean Chrome environments with the target password manager installed, allowing researchers to evaluate compatibility against each minimal working example.

### Technical Details
The authors evaluated the 15 most downloaded password managers on the Chrome Web Store alongside 3 built-in browser vendor managers (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Microsoft Edge). 

Key findings and failure modes include:
- **Failure Rates**: 17 out of the 39 interactions failed to operate seamlessly across more than five password managers. Notably, no single password manager succeeded across all tested interactions.
- **Domain Matching**: Password managers struggle to safely decide whether credentials should be shared across subdomains or related domains without risking credential leakage.
- **Input Field Attributes**: Lack of standardized support or handling for attributes like `autocomplete` or length constraints (e.g., maximum password length).
- **JavaScript Interferences**: Client-side scripts that intercept inputs (such as scripts that capture keystrokes and replace field values with asterisks prior to form submission) or dynamically generated input fields that appear only after explicit user interaction.
- **Complex Form Elements**: Multi-input PIN fields composed of separate HTML tags, split name fields (first name and last name instead of a single username), and pages containing multiple forms simultaneously (such as registration and login forms on one page).

### Takeaways and Proposed Solutions
- **Adoption of Existing Standards**: Many compatibility issues can be resolved immediately if web developers and password managers consistently support existing HTML standards, particularly the `autocomplete` attribute (including support for one-time passcodes / TOTP) and input format specifiers.
- **Emerging Specifications**: Adoption of newer standards, such as Apple's proposed `passwordrules` attribute, can allow websites to explicitly communicate password complexity and character requirements directly to password managers.
- **Credential Sharing Standard**: To address domain matching across subdomains (e.g., `example.com` and `auth.example.com`), the authors propose establishing a new HTTP header or HTML tag mechanism (similar to CSP or CORS). Password managers could issue a lightweight HEAD request to verify whether credential sharing is authorized between origins.
- **Replication Package**: The authors released a replication package containing the minimal working example test site, Selenium scripts, and video recordings demonstrating each tested interaction.

talks.summary:
### Overview
CryptGPU is an end-to-end framework enabling privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) inference and training directly on GPUs. As machine learning models scale from small networks (like LeNet on MNIST) to deeper architectures (such as ResNet and VGG-16 on ImageNet), the primary performance bottleneck shifts from secure multi-party computation (MPC) communication overhead to raw computation, with linear layers accounting for up to 98% of training time in prior work. To bridge the massive performance gap between plain text and private machine learning—which historically reached 23,000x for inference (CryptFlow) and 42,000x for training (Falcon)—CryptGPU keeps all computations on the GPU, yielding substantial speedups across both linear and non-linear layers.

### Key Topics
- **Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML):** Addressing data privacy challenges in collaborative healthcare and diagnostic scenarios where patient data and proprietary model weights must remain confidential during inference and training.
- **Threat Model & Security Assumptions:** Operating under a three-party computation (3PC) framework with semi-honest security and an honest majority, permitting at most one semi-honest corrupt party who follows protocol execution but attempts to learn additional information.
- **Bridging MPC Fixed-Point Arithmetic and GPU CUDA Kernels:** Overcoming the lack of native CUDA kernels for 32-bit or 64-bit integer fixed-point arithmetic by embedding integer operations into floating-point hardware.
- **GPU-Friendly MPC Protocols:** Designing parallel, branch-free non-linear operations (such as approximation-based division and limit-based exponentiation) to maximize GPU parallel execution rather than relying on control-flow-heavy approaches like garbled circuits.

### Technical Details
CryptGPU is built on top of PyTorch and CrypTen, structuring its architecture around three primary pillars:
1. **Replicated Secret Sharing:** Utilizing 3-party replicated additive secret sharing as the core primitive, where each party holds two out of three shares, efficiently supporting addition and multiplication.
2. **Embedding Fixed-Point Arithmetic in Floating-Point Computations:** Standard MPC fixed-point representations require 32-bit or 64-bit integer operations, but standard GPU CUDA acceleration is built around floating-point formats. CryptGPU exploits the fact that 64-bit double-precision floats have 52 bits of precision, enabling exact integer representations between -2^52 and 2^52. Using bilinearity, large integers (32-bit or 64-bit) are decomposed into sums of products of smaller 16-bit integers (e.g., (a1 + a2)(b1 + b2)), ensuring intermediate products never exceed 52 bits and execute without precision loss. This functionality is exposed as a reusable `CudaLongTensor` abstraction.
3. **GPU-Friendly Non-Linear Protocols:** Recognizing that GPUs struggle with conditional branching, CryptGPU replaces branch-heavy garbled circuits with approximation-based methods for private division, and uses limit-based approximations to turn exponentiation into sequences of parallel multiplications.

Empirical evaluations indicate that while CryptGPU shows little benefit on small workloads where communication dominates, it significantly outperforms prior state of the art on larger workloads:
- **Inference:** Delivers a 2.5x to 3.7x improvement over Falcon and CryptFlow on networks such as ResNet and VGG-16 on Tiny ImageNet.
- **Training:** Outperforms Falcon by 7x on small models and up to 36x on large models (e.g., AlexNet on Tiny ImageNet).
- **Microbenchmarks:** Microbenchmark tests reveal that running private convolution on GPU is 100x faster than on CPU, and private ReLU is 10x faster.

### Takeaways
CryptGPU demonstrates that GPU acceleration is critical for practical privacy-preserving machine learning at scale, effectively mitigating the severe computation bottlenecks in linear layer evaluation. While the current system is limited to single-GPU computation, future work includes expanding to multi-GPU clusters and designing dedicated MPC protocols optimized specifically around GPU parallel capabilities.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Method Confusion Attack on the Bluetooth Pairing Process.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Maximilian from churchnets presents a critical vulnerability in Bluetooth pairing protocols called a method confusion attack. As Bluetooth has become the standard for ad hoc device pairing (over 4 billion devices shipped annually as of 2019), it supports numerous device types with varying capabilities and security needs. However, the protocol's complexity to accommodate diverse device classes introduces a fundamental design flaw.

## Key Technical Problem

Bluetooth's pairing process begins with unencrypted interface negotiation, where devices exchange their capabilities and select an appropriate pairing method before establishing secure communication. An attacker can manipulate this negotiation to force two devices into different pairing methods while each believes both are using the same method.

## Pairing Methods Analyzed

Two primary methods are vulnerable:
- **Numeric comparison**: Devices exchange public key material and generate 6-digit decimal hash values displayed on screens. Users visually confirm the values match, authenticating the key material.
- **Pass key entry**: One device generates a random 6-digit value the user transfers to another device, creating a shared secret for secure key exchange.

The critical flaw: numeric comparison values are inherently public (derived from publicly exchanged cryptographic data), while pass key values must remain completely confidential. Both methods exchange indistinguishable 6-digit decimal values.

## Attack Mechanism

The attacker performs pass key entry with device A (prompting the user to input a value) and numeric comparison with device B (displaying the fingerprint). The attacker captures the numeric comparison fingerprint from device B and feeds it into device A as the confidential pass key. This violates pass key entry's security assumption that the value remains confidential, allowing the attacker to complete the zero-knowledge secret key exchange with both devices separately and establish a man-in-the-middle position.

## User Study Results

Researchers conducted a user study where participants performed pairings while the method confusion attack ran silently in the background. No participants detected the attack, even when shown different vendor dialogues, indicating users cannot reliably identify which pairing method is active.

## Mitigation and Future Direction

Current temporary fix: user warnings and clearer UI indication of the pairing method. However, this cannot prevent the attack. The researchers are developing tools to analyze protocols for such flaws and creating a new protocol that supports multiple pairing methods while being formally verifiable to exclude such design vulnerabilities.

talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Steve on behalf of a research collaboration between the University of Illinois, Virginia Tech, and Shape Security, this talk focuses on developing machine learning (ML) models for cybersecurity when labeled data is scarce. Using bot detection as a primary case study—covering threats like account takeover and web scraping—the presentation addresses three major challenges: the scarcity of ground-truth labels, concept drift caused by evolving attacker behavior, and the poor generalizability of highly customized domain features across different web services.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Bot Detection Strategy:** The architecture prioritizes rule-based detection for high-precision, low-cost coverage of common bots, deploying machine learning specifically to catch advanced bots that evade static rules by mutating their behavior.
- **Frequency-Based Feature Encoding:** Replacing raw application-specific features with generic network features (e.g., URL, cookie, browser), converted dynamically into frequency distributions using cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) over a sliding window.
- **Neural Data Augmentation:** A specialized dual-generator Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture tailored for security contexts where benign data is representative, but malicious data is scarce, biased, and rapidly shifting.

### Technical Details
- **Dataset & Ground Truth:** The research evaluated 23 million network requests collected across three distinct websites (A, B, and C) spanning three months of data over a one-year period. Ground-truth labels were primarily established via user CAPTCHA interactions.
- **Feature Processing:** To avoid raw string dependencies and generalize across services, features are encoded based on frequency percentiles in an empirical CDF. A daily sliding window updates the distribution dynamically to handle unseen items and concept drift in real time.
- **Data Synthesis Architecture:** Standard GANs merely mimic existing samples, which fails against adapting bots. The proposed method splits malicious samples into clusters and outliers using DBSCAN:
  1. *Cluster Data Synthesis:* Synthesizes data near existing bot clusters by expanding boundaries cautiously, becoming less aggressive near benign data regions.
  2. *Outlier Data Synthesis:* Aggressively synthesizes data outward in the complementary space outside benign regions to anticipate future bot variants.
  3. *Discriminator Role:* Functions as the downstream classifier trained to differentiate benign users from both real and synthetic malicious bots.

### Takeaways
- **Rule and ML Complementarity:** Rule-based detection captured roughly 80% of bots, while adding the ML pipeline boosted detection to over 90%.

talks.summary:
Zhu Jianping presents HETD, a heterogeneous trusted execution environment designed to enable rack-scale confidential computing in data centers without chip-level modifications. The motivation addresses the need to protect pooled computing resources (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs) commonly distributed across modern data centers, where existing TEE solutions either require hardware changes or cannot efficiently support such architectures.

The HETD system architecture consists of a sealed chassis containing a security controller (SSC based on MCPU and FPGA), PCI Express fabric for resource management, multiple proxy microservice nodes with accelerators, and untrusted external server nodes. The design separates security functions (in SSC) from computation (in HETD enclaves running standard software like TensorFlow and GPU drivers), minimizing the trusted computing base.

Key technical components include elastic resource allocation via PCIe fabric's software-defined and flexible topology properties, secure enclave lifecycle management through secure reboot procedures that clear memory and reset accelerators, and data protection using AES-GCM encryption with separate message queues for ciphertext and plaintext areas. An FPGA-based cryptographic controller enforces isolation, with no direct shared space between components. Trust establishment uses a two-layer public key design (endorsement key and attestation key) with remote attestation and symmetric key negotiation.

The threat model considers a strong adversary controlling the software stack and capable of side-channel attacks via network traffic analysis. Physical snooping on the host memory bus is in scope but not within the sealed HETD box. Covert channels, attacks on cryptographic algorithms, and denial-of-service attacks are out of scope.

The prototype integrates two Xilinx PX 9797 boards, one SC node, four processor nodes, and four NVIDIA GPUs. Performance evaluation shows throughput overhead under 5% for most workloads, with batch-size-dependent latency overhead reaching 42.96% for inference and 18.54% for training at batch size 8. Encryption overhead is small and stable. Multiple-GPU scalability matches the baseline, demonstrating that elastic resource allocation can improve single-enclave performance without sacrificing horizontal scalability.

The system provides four security guarantees in a Platform-as-a-Service model: isolation from other enclaves on the same proxy node, isolation from past and future users, protection from untrusted hosts, and protection from cloud providers. The design resists side-bleed attacks on sealed FPGAs and cold boot attacks when unauthorized chassis opening takes longer than power-removal-based memory extraction.
